newsitem.title: INDIA: FUND VIEW - Indian mutual funds battle negative image.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Indian mutual funds battle negative image.

text.p: India's mutual funds will continue to face sceptical investors until strong performances erase the public's unhappy memories of unfulfilled expectations, the chief of Birla Capital Asset Management Co said on Monday.
A deepening political crisis in New Delhi will not help their cause, analysts said.
"The industry's difficult phase will continue for some time," Ramamoorthy Ganesh, chief executive officer of Birla Capital International AMC Ltd told Reuters in an interview.
India's stock markets boomed in March after the government announced an industry-friendly budget for financial year 1997/98, running from April to March.

But share prices crashed last week after the Congress Party said it was withdrawing support to the ruling United Front government. The minority coalition faces a confidence vote on Friday with its budget still to be passed, and analysts expect political turmoil to plague capital markets in the near-term.
Birla Capital, a joint venture of Aditya Birla Group and U.S. fund manager Capital International, is India's largest private sector open-ended mutual fund, established in 1995.
Two open-ended mutual funds, one focusing on equities and the other bonds, from DSP Merrill Lynch, the Indian affiliate of the U.S. investment bank, opened for subscription on Monday.
Ganesh said only a strong performance will erase the negative public view of mutual funds. "The negative image has to be first neutralised, then we can move to positive territory."
"We recently went for a one percent exposure to equity in our Birla Income Plus, but there was so much negative feedback that we decided to stick to 100 percent debt," he said.

He said the fact equity exposure raised a scare among professionals, high income individuals and trusts -- usually the most informed investors -- showed how deep rooted was the bias against equity investments.
The Bombay Stock Exchange 30-share index -- India's most visible stock index -- fell from a high of 4,643.31 on September 12, 1994, to a low of 2,713.12 on December 4, 1996.
"Morgan Stanley continues to haunt the industry," said an investment manager of another mutual fund, referring to a close-ended fund launched by 1994 when stock prices had peaked.
The retail public response to Morgan Stanley issue had exceeded all expectations, collecting over 9.0 billion rupees compared to an initial target of 3.0 billion.
Investors across India are now stuck with their investment as Morgan Stanley is quoted below the issue price.

Some mutual funds which have declared good results for the year ended March 31, 1997 have been able to do so by turning the focus away from equities to debt market instruments, like corporate debentures and bonds.

"Our strategy has been to minimise losses rather than maximise profits," Nimesh Kampani, chairman of JM Group of companies said last week, referring to JM Mutual Fund, which invested in fixed income schemes to ensure that investors' capital was protected despite falling share prices.

Birla Mutual's maiden fund Birla Advantage, with its main focus on equities, has crossed the one billion rupees mark. Its second launch Birla Income Plus, has crossed 2.0 billion rupees from the starting figure of 560 million rupees in October 1995, chief executive officer Ganesh said.
Birla Mutual calls its 12 regional marketing offices "business development offices" which promotes the mutual fund concept apart from its two open-end schemes.
Some 10 companies have signed up with Birla Mutual to allow monthly deduction towards Birla Mutual's growth schemes.
"We don't want to have guaranteed returns," Ganesh said. "Then what's the difference between mutual fund and a fixed deposit?"
Birla Mutual Fund wanted to attract investors through its track record and service to investors, he said.
-- Bombay Newsroom, (91) 22 265 9000
